Title: Interview with lululemon's former VP accessoriess

URL Source: https://embeddedbrandstrategy.substack.com/p/how-to-engineer-a-product-into-a

Published Time: 2026-08-16T14:45:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
“_How do we launch our next hit product_?”

I’ve been asked this in nearly every role I’ve had: at P&G, Son of a Tailor, Blank Street, and now at Business of Fashion (BoF). Brands need hit products to grow, but launching them can feel like a mix of strategy and luck.

A year ago a handbag client asked me to help them launch the next ‘it’ bag. I had a budget to bring in outside expertise, and I knew exactly who I wanted to speak with: **[Dennis Wang](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dennis-wang-842b7025).**

Wang built the accessories division at lululemon from zero to over a billion dollars (yes, with a B!) and has led accessories design at TUMI, Kate Spade, Coach, and Michael Kors. He understands how to design products that thread the needle of feeling familiar to the brand while also delivering on a technical innovation, and how to work across marketing and merchandising to ensure a product succeeds commercially.

He was generous enough to speak about his process with me again, on the record. The conversation is below.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WLsC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F783e0925-912c-451d-b277-57d7fd1bdcd9_729x948.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WLsC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F783e0925-912c-451d-b277-57d7fd1bdcd9_729x948.jpeg)

**Tell us about yourself: what do you do, and what’s the unfair advantage you bring to it?**

My name is Dennis Wang, and I run a brand and advisory practice, DWAN (Dream, Wake, And Navigate). Prior to founding my consultancy, I spent 20+ years working in accessories design at TUMI, Kate Spade, Coach, Michael Kors, and most recently, as Vice President of Accessories Design at lululemon.

The unfair advantage I bring to product design is an ability to apply logical frameworks to creativity. In this industry, there is a temptation to let personal ego, emotion, and fleeting inspiration drive the creative process. But treating design only as self-expression turns product development into a guessing game.

When you apply logic to design, commercial success becomes an engineered outcome. This philosophy is the foundation of my practice and the thesis of my upcoming book, _The Lost Math of Design_.

**What does applying this logic to a brand look like in practice?**

Many companies treat the brand as a visual veneer to drive short term sales, obsessing over SKUs, color palettes, celebrity endorsements, and marketing campaigns.

True brand building requires going deeper to execute what I call C.P.R.: finding the pulse of the Customer, engineering the Product to solve their specific friction, and generating Relevancy within the user experience.

**How did you apply the C.P.R. framework to build the accessories department at lululemon, a fitness brand with no accessories?**

The realization actually came when I was at Michael Kors. The CEO asked us: _“Why are our customers getting older, and why can’t we attract a younger generation?”_ I answered by developing seven entirely new concepts spanning athletic, travel, sustainability, and broader lifestyle elements to inject relevance into the brand. It was rejected with a single sentence: _“That’s not who we are.”_

It was a classic Innovator’s Dilemma. Legacy brands stagnate when they become too protective of their past.

Then I looked at lululemon. Running them through my C.P.R. framework, I saw they already had absolute dominance with the Customer and cultural Relevancy. They just needed a Product to complete the daily lifestyle loop. The bag is the physical bridge between fitness and the rest of their day.

On the last day of a holiday in Vancouver, I asked my family’s permission and submitted my resume like a lottery ticket. I pitched myself as a creative leader who could build that bridge. If you look at the industry, every major designer label has had to evolve into a full lifestyle ecosystem to survive. lululemon already owned the culture of movement; they simply needed to build the tools for the rest of their customer’s journey.

Every major designer label has had to evolve into a full lifestyle ecosystem to survive.

**Why do you think your pitch was successful?**

It is tempting to say my pitch succeeded because I walked in with a 100-page presentation on vision and strategy. The truth is it it succeeded because of the trust of the former CPO, Sun Choe. My deck proved the math of the business, but Sun Choe trusted my instinct and vision as a creative leader to actually build the architecture.

When you have an executive who fully empowers you and trusts your vision without micromanaging the “how,” it unlocks something powerful.

**How did you keep these executives believing before the numbers arrived?**

I operated like a weed, without a massive budget or a large headcount.

But flying under the radar turned out to be our greatest advantage. Instead of fighting for internal capital and pitching for permission, we treated the division like a stealth startup and stayed focused on building. I pulled every string from decades in the industry, leveraging external vendors, calling in favors with suppliers, and hacking together unique production processes completely off-grid.

When the accessories business crossed a billion dollars and the [Everywhere Belt Bag](https://go.shopmy.us/p-79523194) went viral, the company was genuinely shocked. Calvin, the CEO at the time, was surprised by a massive revenue engine he barely had to manage. Sometimes the best way to build a disruptive category isn’t to demand a seat at the corporate table, it’s to build something undeniable in the shadows.

Flying under the radar was our greatest advantage. Instead of fighting for internal capital, we treated the division like a stealth startup and focused on building.

**What was the design process for the bestselling [Everywhere Belt Bag](https://go.shopmy.us/p-79523194)?**

The brief was quite humble: design a bag for the lululemon “educators” working the store floor. They needed to carry absolute essentials while keeping their hands completely free to support guests.

Then the pandemic hit. Overnight, the entire world shared the exact same psychological need as our store educators: a demand for only the essentials, completely hands-free.

**Creating hit products (like the Everywhere Belt Bag) is never guaranteed. How can you stack the odds in your favor?**

The real secret to great design is simple: hunt for a problem.

Then, to stack the odds, every design must pass a ruthless filter. It must do at least one of three things: make a profit, tell a story, or make a statement. If you find the right problem and engineer a product that hits all three simultaneously, you aren’t leaving anything to chance.

A new product must do at least one of three things: make a profit, tell a story, or make a statement. Ideally all three simultaneously.

**If a private equity firm gave you 24 months and a budget to stand up a new category inside a portfolio company, what would you need on day one?**

Most teams panic about the clock and rush straight into designing products to show early momentum. That is a trap. You cannot build a category without knowing exactly who you are and what specific human friction you are solving.

On Day 1, I don’t look at the budget, and I don’t look at the product. I demand total clarity on one non-negotiable asset: the Persona. If it’s broken, we fix it. If it doesn’t exist, we build it. The Persona dictates the Vision. The Vision dictates the Strategy. The Strategy dictates the Execution.

You cannot build a category without knowing exactly who you are and what specific human friction you are solving.

Only when that architecture is locked do I deploy my 90-day operational playbook: evaluate the People, streamline the Process, engineer the Product, and drive the Profit.

**Once you have a great product, you have to market it. If you had to kill every marketing channel but one, what survives?**

I would keep the Community / Partnerships channel. Most companies reduce this channel to “influencer marketing.” They treat people like human billboards. It is a fleeting, hollow tactic that drives a transactional spike at best.

Instead, you want to operate this channel through the lens of a Muse. In Jungian terms, a Muse is the living embodiment of your brand’s psychological archetype (the “C” in my C.P.R. framework). People don’t connect with algorithms, SEO, or paid ad channels; they connect with people. A flawlessly engineered product paired with a Muse who embodies your audience’s collective unconscious will outlive and outperform any digital channel on earth.

People don’t connect with algorithms, SEO, or paid ad channels; they connect with people.

**Which company’s marketing are you most jealous of right now, and why?**

Coach.

A few years ago, Coach was dangerously close to becoming a relic. When heritage brands hit that wall, they panic and throw money at arbitrary celebrity endorsements or aggressively redesign the product until it becomes unrecognizable.

Coach didn’t do that. They executed a masterclass in the “R” of my C.P.R. framework: Relevancy. They realized the product wasn’t the problem; the psychology was. By leaning into initiatives like Coachtopia and narrative-driven Gen Z campaigns, they tapped directly into the collective unconscious of an entirely new demographic. Through comms, they turned a heritage bag into a modern canvas for self-expression.

[![Image 2: Coach Tests 'Circular' Coachtopia Sub-Brand | BoF](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pCGl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5061a692-5814-4952-8429-139275d7a171_1440x812.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pCGl!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5061a692-5814-4952-8429-139275d7a171_1440x812.jpeg)

Coachtopia

That level of cultural engineering is incredibly difficult to execute, and absolutely worth being jealous of.

**Kate Spade, your former employer, recently hired a new Creative Director as part of a larger plan to reinvigorate the brand. What advice would you give to him (or anyone else) attempting to bring a brand back to cultural and commercial relevance?**

Kate Spade remains the longest tenure of my career because, at our peak, we operated as a flawless triad: Vision, Strategy, and Execution.

Deborah provided the visionary storytelling. I provided the execution, translating her vivid ideas into physical architecture. Our merchants drove the commercial strategy. It was a perfectly balanced machine. But the fatal trap for any legacy brand is assuming a machine that worked in the past will automatically work today.

My advice to the new leadership goes right back to my Day 1 playbook: you must ruthlessly audit and update the Persona. The original Kate Spade was famously fun and whimsical, but that specific lifestyle doesn’t match the reality of the current generation. The world moved, and the persona didn’t.

You cannot reinvigorate a heritage brand by simply dusting off the archives. You have to redefine the Persona for the modern woman’s actual daily friction and rebuild that triad—Vision, Strategy, and Execution—to serve exactly who she is today.

The original Kate Spade was famously fun and whimsical, but that specific lifestyle doesn’t match the reality of the current generation.

**If you had capital and could buy one brand today, what would you buy, and what would you do in the first year?**

There are three types of brands: Brand > Product, Product > Brand, and Brand = Product. The ROI lives entirely in the imbalances.

If a brand has incredible marketing but a mediocre product, customer churn will eventually kill it. If it has brilliant engineering but a weak persona, it gets buried by louder competitors. Year One is simply diagnosing the deficit and fixing the weaker half.

If I had the capital, I would target three specific imbalances right now:

*   **[Béis](https://go.shopmy.us/p-79523371) (Travel):**_Brand > Product._ The cultural heat is phenomenal. Bring in rigorous structural engineering to elevate the physical product, and it scales exponentially.

*   **[Brooks Running](https://go.shopmy.us/p-79523661) (Footwear):**_Product > Brand._ The engineering is flawless, but they missed the cultural wave captured by On and Hoka. Upgrade the cosmetic execution and brand storytelling, and it’s an immediate win.

*   **[Varley](https://go.shopmy.us/p-79523754) (Apparel):**_Product > Brand._ The industry thinks athleisure was a trend; it was actually a permanent evolution in fabrication. Varley is successfully bridging technical athletic fabrics with modern ready-to-wear. Year One is about taking that flawless product architecture and amplifying the brand persona to a global scale.

When you acquire a brand where the foundation is strong and you only have to fix one side of the equation, whether it’s elevating the architecture or amplifying the persona, you aren’t gambling. **You are just doing the math**.

Wang’s ability to ‘do the math’ on brand value is unmatched; during the editing process of this interview Samsonite agreed to acquire Béis at a $210M valuation.

What do you think of Wang’s C.P.R. framework? I personally love it. Great brands aren’t just cultural heat, and they aren’t just great product. They’re both. But engineering that starts with a shared understanding of the customer. Building that customer persona is something we did in the Blank Street brand repositioning, refocusing the brand from targeting ‘_everyone_’ to a clear picture of the Blank Street girl: Gen Z, interested in wellness, little treats, and social media. One your muse is clear, product and relevance can flow.

I have a few more interviews from brand operators coming up. Subscribe to get them in your inbox.

Contact Dennis here, and keep an eye out for his book!

Title: How We Built a Recognizable, Scalable Brand in Brooklyn’s Crowded Food Scene

URL Source: https://dribbble.com/stories/2026/08/21/cl-paul-lilley-ulysses-recognizable-scalable-brand

Markdown Content:
About the Author:

_Paul Lilley,_[_Ulysses_](https://www.ulyssesdesignco.com/)_Founder / Creative Director, cut his teeth in London and Melbourne working for creative and art agencies including Vice, Cornerstone, and Next Wave. His collaborations with international clients on large scale campaigns gave him deep grounding in strategy, positioning and brand identity design, which he now brings directly to food and beverage founders building their brands._

To be a restaurant owner in the foodie borough that is Brooklyn, NY, you should be ready to compete not just on the quality of your food, but also on experience, atmosphere, service, social media, and branding. Ultimately, these touchpoints decide whether somebody remembers your restaurant when they’re deciding where to go on Friday night.

That was the challenge we faced when we were approached to create the brand for [Lucky Parlor](https://www.ulyssesdesignco.com/projects/lucky-parlor-gyoza-bar), a new gyoza and cocktail bar in Brooklyn.

**The owner, Tatsumi, found us through Dribbble.**

He’d seen our profile and examples of how we’d helped other food and beverage businesses build distinctive brands in similarly crowded markets, and our approach resonated with what he wanted to create.

This wasn’t Tatsumi’s first restaurant. The team already operated two Japanese food concepts in Brooklyn and had built a local reputation around high-quality, more traditional Japanese sushi and udon. But this time they wanted to push the boat out a little further.

![Image 1](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-4-846x420.png)
Lucky Parlor wasn’t supposed to be just another place to eat gyoza. The vision was a neighborhood hangout: somewhere you could drop into any night of the week with friends, family, or by yourself. The menu would combine creative, small-plate Japanese food with equally interesting contemporary cocktails, all served in an environment that felt relaxed but still elevated.

**Our job was to make the brand feel as interesting as the concept.** We didn’t need to create another nice-looking restaurant. We needed to make it unmistakably Lucky Parlor.

## **Building a brand before a logo.**

The initial request was branding. And from the get-go, we knew it wasn’t just a logo. This is an important distinction because one of the biggest mistakes I see businesses—and sometimes designers—make is treating the logo as the brand.

A logo is an identifier. It’s one piece of a much larger system. Lucky Parlor needed a flexible brand capable of growing with the business.

Our scope began with brand strategy, followed by the identity: logo, typography, color, illustration, brand assets, collateral, and a website as the brand’s digital home. Our pitch was simple: **don’t invest in a logo; invest in a brand that’s built to scale.**

![Image 2](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lucky-parlor-dribbble-menu-1-846x420.jpg)
A restaurant needs to show up in dozens of places: menus, signage, packaging, social media, merchandise, events, digital touchpoints, and applications nobody can predict on day one. If the entire identity depends on putting the logo in the corner, you haven’t really built a brand system. You’ve built a logo and a collection of layouts.

We wanted to give Lucky Parlor a recognizable visual language its audience could connect with across all of those touchpoints. The test for us was simple: **if you removed the logo, would somebody still recognize the brand?**

![Image 3](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lucky-parlor-dribbble-logo-3-846x420.jpg)
## **Letting strategy drive every design decision.**

Before we drew anything, we defined what Lucky Parlor needed to become. Our project goal was to position it as a **friendly and innovative gyoza bar serving some of the best Japanese food and contemporary cocktails in the game.**

The concept sat somewhere between a gyoza bar, a cocktail bar, and a tapas-style dining experience. The owners wanted to create a place that brought people together around a shared love of handcrafted gyoza, creative small plates, and modern interpretations of familiar cocktails.

That gave us some useful tensions to work with: **friendly, but elevated. Playful, but premium. Creative, but not chaotic. Innovative, but still accessible.**

Those tensions became much more useful than a collection of visual references.

![Image 4](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lucky-parlor-dribbble-menu-846x420.jpg)
This is why I believe strategy should come before aesthetics. **Strategy doesn’t restrict creativity; it gives creativity a problem worth solving.** Without strategy, the conversation becomes, “Do we like this font?” With strategy, it becomes, “Does this font help us feel playful but premium?”

That’s a much better conversation.

The same applies to every design decision. Instead of asking whether something simply looks cool, we can ask whether it moves the brand closer to the position we’re trying to own. Our filter throughout the project became incredibly simple: **Does this feel like Lucky Parlor?**

![Image 5](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lucky-parlor-dribbble-instagram-stories-846x420.jpg)
## **Exploring the right amount of spice.**

Once the strategy was established, we moved into creative exploration. Our approach is highly collaborative. We don’t believe the best way to get to a strong solution is to disappear for a few weeks, come back with one polished direction, and announce, “Here it is.”

Instead, we explore a spectrum. Internally, we call it **mild, medium, and spicy**.

Mild gives the client a relatively safe interpretation of the strategy. Medium pushes things further. Spicy asks what happens if we really lean into the personality and see how far the idea can go. Importantly, these aren’t three random logos. They’re three interpretations of the same strategic foundation.

For Lucky Parlor, our first direction was more minimal and hand-drawn, taking inspiration from the visual character of a Japanese postcard. It was charming and considered, but deliberately restrained.

![Image 6](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-11-846x420.png)
The second direction became bolder. We explored bold typography with a drop shadow, inspired by vintage signwriting and old Brooklyn storefronts. It had more physical presence and brought some of the neighborhood energy into the identity.

The third pushed the personality furthest. We explored playful, nostalgic-inspired lettering and reinterpreted it through a contemporary lens. It felt friendly, energetic, and recognizable without losing the elevated quality we wanted. That became the foundation for the final identity.

But presenting the work wasn’t a matter of, “Here are three options. Pick one.” A client might respond to the energy of one direction, the typography of another, or a detail from the third. Our job is to understand _why_ they’re responding to those things and use that information to refine the brand.

We’re not asking the client to become the designer. **We’re using their reactions as data.**

![Image 7](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-5-846x420.png)
## **Creating a world around one gyoza mark.**

The centerpiece of the identity became a simple gyoza brand mark. Rather than plastering it over everything, it became a recurring shape and visual device throughout the system. It could function as a recognizable mark, a frame, a graphic device, or a small detail that tied an application back to the wider brand.

That repetition matters. A distinctive brand isn’t created by inventing something new every time you design an application. It’s created by identifying a small number of recognizable ingredients and using them consistently enough that people start associating those ingredients with you.

![Image 8](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-13-846x420.png)
We paired the core identity with an extended palette of vibrant but slightly muted colors, while black became a consistent grounding element. It allowed the identity to be colorful without becoming childish and playful without losing its premium edge.

Another major part of the system was illustration. We created a suite of hand-drawn illustrations covering everything from gyoza and cocktails to illustrations inspired by the founder’s daughters. The style was deliberately naive, loose, and imperfect.

![Image 9](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-7-846x420.png)
Those subtle imperfections were important. In branding, perfection isn’t always the answer. Sometimes making everything perfectly geometric, perfectly aligned, and perfectly consistent strips out the thing people would have connected with.

The hand-drawn quality gave Lucky Parlor warmth and provided another ownable ingredient that could stretch across collateral, merchandise, digital applications, and future communications.

This is something we prioritize in our work. Custom typography, illustration, lettering, textures, and graphic devices add a human touch that creates a brand capable of standing out in a crowded market.

## **Designing for what we couldn’t predict.**

The brand will eventually appear somewhere you didn’t anticipate. Somebody will need a poster tomorrow. A new menu will launch. There will be merchandise, an event, a collaboration, a social post, a new location, or some other application that wasn’t in the original scope.

You can’t design all of those things in advance. What you _can_ design is a system capable of handling them.

For Lucky Parlor, the gyoza mark, typography, color palette, illustrations, textures, and graphic language became a box of ingredients. Those ingredients could be combined differently depending on the application without losing the thread of the brand.

This is where I think [designers](https://dribbble.com/designers) need to rethink what consistency means. **Consistency doesn’t mean making everything look the same. It means making everything feel like it came from the same place.**

![Image 10](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/lucky-parlor-dribbble-macbook-pro-846x420.jpg)
If every piece of communication is identical, the brand becomes boring. If every piece is completely different, the brand becomes forgettable. The opportunity lives somewhere in the middle.

When we’re building identities, I’m interested in creating what I think of as **memory hooks**: a small number of distinctive elements customers can begin associating with the business. For Lucky Parlor, the gyoza mark is one. The lettering is another. The illustration style, color palette, and overall playfulness create others.

Individually, none of those elements has to carry the entire identity. Together, they create recognition. The first time someone sees the brand, they notice it. The next time, it feels familiar. Eventually, they recognize Lucky Parlor before they’ve consciously processed the name.

That’s when design starts becoming brand equity.

## **Giving Lucky Parlor a sense of self.**

Lucky Parlor was a business concept with a clear vision but without a visual identity capable of expressing it. Afterward, it had a sense of self.

The brand became friendly, recognizable, playful, and distinctive. More importantly, the founders had a visual system they could continue using as the restaurant grew.

That, to me, is the real deliverable of a branding project. Yes, we delivered logos, typography, colors, illustrations, collateral, and all of the tangible assets you’d expect. But the more important result was clarity. The business knew how it should show up, what it should feel like, and had the tools to communicate that consistently.

![Image 11](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-9-846x420.png)
**We didn’t just create another gyoza restaurant. We created Lucky Parlor.**

That’s the difference I want branding to make.

## **Giving people a reason to remember.**

**My biggest advice to designers and agencies hoping to win projects like Lucky Parlor is to stop leading with deliverables.**

Clients can find thousands of people capable of designing a nice logo. What they have a much harder time finding is somebody who can understand why their business is struggling to differentiate itself and translate that problem into a brand people remember.

Ask them the following:

*   Who they’re competing against
*   What customers should remember about them
*   What conventions dominate their category
*   Where they want to fit in and where they deliberately want to break away
*   What they want people saying about the business when they’re not in the room

Then design.

And when you present the work, don’t just explain what you made. Explain **why**. “We used hand-drawn illustrations because they look cool” is an aesthetic explanation. “We used hand-drawn illustrations because the imperfection gives the brand the warmth and approachability required by the positioning” is a strategic explanation.

Same illustration. Very different conversation. The first positions you as someone who makes things look good. The second positions you as someone who can solve business problems through design.

![Image 12](https://content-hub.dribbble.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-10-846x420.png)
**Lastly, for brands facing the same challenge as Lucky Parlor, I’d pay close attention to the questions designers and agencies ask before they talk about aesthetics.**

A [good branding partner](https://dribbble.com/hire/brand-designers) should want to understand your business, audience, competitive environment, personality, ambitions, and the space you can realistically own.

They should also be willing to push you. The objective isn’t to hire somebody who agrees with everything you say. It’s to find someone who can take what you know about your business, combine it with an outsider perspective, and identify opportunities you might not see from inside the company.

Because ultimately, branding isn’t about having the prettiest logo in your category.

**It’s about giving people a reason to notice you, a reason to remember you, and a reason to choose you.**

And in a crowded market, that might be the most valuable thing a brand can own.

_If you resonate with this article or would like to hear what Ulysses Design Co can do for your brand, you can drop me a line [here.](https://www.ulyssesdesignco.com/elevate-my-brand)_

kept.heading: BRAND HYPE HAS EXISTED SINCE THE BRONZE AGE, SCIENTISTS DISCOVER (5 MINUTE READ)

Title: Brand Hype Has Existed Since the Bronze Age, Scientists Discover

URL Source: https://www.404media.co/brand-hype-has-existed-since-the-bronze-age-scientists-discover/

Published Time: 2026-08-22T10:00:35.000Z

Markdown Content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that pottered around, ate well, shone bright, and went long in the tooth.

First, scientists identified a Bronze Age tradition of pottery as one of the earliest “brands,” revealing that humanity’s love for reliable commodities has deep roots. Then: a meal fit for a galaxy, a multi-camera view of the Sun, and a dizzying deep dive into a narwhal tusk.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book [_First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens_](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/becky-ferreira/first-contact/9781523527755/?ref=404media.co), or subscribe to my personal newsletter [the BeX Files](https://bexfiles.ghost.io/?ref=404media.co).

## **Brands are not brand new**

[_Luciani, Marta et al. “Creating a brand. Genesis, transformation and diffusion of Qurayyah Painted Ware.” PLOS One._](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0351296&ref=404media.co)

Brands have completely taken over the modern world, from established corporate trademarks to the proliferation of online influencers. But the allure of brands is nothing new, according to a study about an ancient style of pottery called Qurayyah Painted Ware that was a progenitor of branding some 3,200 years ago.

This brand of pottery was popular in what is now Saudi Arabia during the Bronze Age. The tradition is distinguished by distinctive black-and-red geometric designs and stylized animal and human figures. These unique visual properties, along with a consistent production technique and quality, suggest that it was an early branded commodity that was made to be recognizable to the wider community.

“It is now understood that brands and proto-brands existed well before modern economies,” said researchers led by Marta Luciani of the University of Vienna. “In this contribution we analyze the process by which the commodity itself—decorated pottery vessels—was developed into a brand not by added symbols but on the virtue of its visual identity, material consistency, technological continuity, centralized production, export circulation, local imitation, intentional commercial scope, and cultural reputation.”

As such, the study “offers the first investigation of the dynamics leading to the genesis of a brand,” the team concluded.

Now, that’s a vintage brand. Who wants to do the sponsored endorsement on socials?

## **A low-energy snack for the Milky Way**

[_Massari, Davide et al. “Evidence of a massive accretion event 1.8 billion years before the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger.” Nature Astronomy._](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02931-5?ref=404media.co)

Our home galaxy, the Milky Way, extends across 100,000 light years and contains hundreds of billions of stars. How did it get so swole? The answer is a healthy diet made up of smaller galaxies that the Milky Way has swallowed over time, adding to its starry heft.

Now, scientists have identified the digested remains of a galaxy that served as cosmic baby food for the Milky Way during its infancy some 12 billion years ago. By studying stars at the center of the galaxy using the Hubble Space Telescope, the team was able to reconstruct this ancient merger between the Milky Way and a dwarf galaxy that has been gifted with the amazing name “Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles” (LKH) after its constituent parts.

[![Image 1](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-d0410647-5076-4fb4-90b9-eacc737affb3.jpeg)](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-d0410647-5076-4fb4-90b9-eacc737affb3.jpeg)

_\_Concept art of Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles merging with the Milky Way 12 billion years ago. Image: NASA, ESA, Joseph Olmsted (STScI)\__

“Our conclusions are strongly supported by cosmological simulations, which typically predict between one and four substantial mergers in the history of a Milky Way-like galaxy,” said researchers led by Davide Massari of the Observatory of Bologna. “The identification of a third merger event in the inner Galaxy puts to rest earlier debates and, honouring previous works, we name the progenitor system Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles, or LKH for short.”

The study explains the origins of a group of metal-poor stars in the galactic center suggesting that they are leftovers from the LKH galaxy, which was about as massive as 500 million Suns. This merger occurred before the engulfment of another fantastically-named galaxy, Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus, which occurred about 10 billion years ago and significantly influenced the Milky Way’s evolution.

It goes to show that you are what you eat (in this case, yummy primordial galaxies).

## **The Sun goes ka-blowie**

[_Luspay-Kuti, Adrienn et al. “The structure of a complex, asymmetric coronal mass ejection revealed by 17 spacecraft across the inner heliosphere.” Science Advances._](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed9960?ref=404media.co)

It’s time, once again, to pay tribute to the almighty Sun. Our star regularly barfs out enormous streams of solar plasma known as coronal mass ejections (CMEs), which radiate across the solar system and can wreak havoc on satellites and even ground infrastructure in some cases.

But while these solar blowouts are common, their underlying mechanics are still poorly understood. Now, scientists report unprecedented observations of a CME that occurred in December 2024, which was captured by 17 spacecraft. In particular, measurements from NASA’s Europa Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter’s icy ocean moon, revealed “a structure far more complex than could be inferred from single-point observations,” according to the study.

[![Image 2](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-f2590251-03c7-4e0a-8efe-7c8add852238.jpeg)](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-f2590251-03c7-4e0a-8efe-7c8add852238.jpeg)

_\_Images of the December 2024 CME. Image:\__[_\_Luspay-Kuti, Adrienn et al.\__](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed9960?ref=404media.co)

“This study demonstrates the power of coordinated multipoint observations to uncover the true complexity of CME evolution in the inner heliosphere,” said researchers led by

Adrienn Luspay-Kuti of Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. “Such structure would not have been resolvable from Sun-Earth line observations alone. As human exploration extends toward Mars, such comprehensive heliospheric coverage will be critical for protecting spacecraft and crew.”

As if future crews to Mars don’t have enough to worry about, they’ll also have to take cover from projectile star vomit. At least the complex workings of CMEs are gradually becoming illuminated, though we may never fully understand these mercurial outbursts.

## **Taking a tusk to task**

[_Rodriguez-Palomo, Adrian et al. “The narwhal tusk assembles its macroscopic helix from building blocks with opposing twists.” Nature Communications._](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75689-z?ref=404media.co)

Speaking of structures that get more complicated under close inspection, may I interest you in a narwhal’s tusk? These elegant elongated ornaments have inspired many myths and legends due to their unicorn-like appearance, and they have also enraptured scientists for generations.

A team has now unraveled the mysterious layers of the narwhal tusk using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, which allowed them to resolve its structure on atomic, nano, and micro scales. The examination of the tusk confirmed that it consists of a left-facing helix, whereas another interior structure twists to the right. This mesh is sculpted with small deviations that mirror the iconic twisted spiral of the tusk.

[![Image 3](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-0dfe1473-de0a-4933-9966-1ba24a12669f.jpeg)](https://storage.ghost.io/c/0f/76/0f76b548-bc58-4f25-abc3-3f5ebca07da4/content/images/2026/08/data-src-image-0dfe1473-de0a-4933-9966-1ba24a12669f.jpeg)

_\_This 3D image shows how the mineralized collagen fibrils – the microscopic building blocks that give the tooth its strength – are arranged. Image: Adrian Rodriguez Palomo / Nature Communications\__

“To finally solve the narwhal helical tusk puzzle, we combine multimodal imaging and multiscale orientation analysis, enabling accurate mapping of the tusk from the atomic to the macroscopic scale,” said researchers led by Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo of Aarhus University.

“The structural anisotropy and the ensuing anisotropic mechanics mean that the tusk can grow straight, unlike, e.g., the curved elephant tusk, providing the narwhal with its majestic, evocative defining characteristic,” the team concluded. “The formation of such a structure remains unknown, as we lack crucial information on narwhal tusk growth and development.”

Shout out to all the aspiring narwhal scientists out there—looks like there’s more work to do.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

kept.heading: HERE'S HOW TO BUILD YOUR MARKETING TEAM FOR THE AI ERA (4 MINUTE READ)

Title: A New Report Says Hiring Marketers Has Changed for Good. Here’s How to Build Your Marketing Team for the AI Era

URL Source: https://www.inc.com/ashley-couto/hiring-marketing-team-ai-era-startup-founders/91393348

Published Time: 2026-08-21T10:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
It’s no surprise that the role of [marketers](https://www.inc.com/nicole-ramirez/marketers-consulting-collectives-career-trend/91304763) is changing quickly. Now, the American [Marketing](https://www.inc.com/marketing "Marketing") Association’s recently released [State of Marketing Careers Report](https://resources.ama.org/2026-state-of-marketing-careers-report) sheds new light on how marketers’ roles are morphing.

According to the report, [marketing](https://www.inc.com/kevin-j-ryan/marketing-strategy-dreamday-adler-local-ladidadi/91220442) job postings are still down 27 percent from their pre-pandemic peak while the share of postings mentioning [AI](https://www.inc.com/artificial-intelligence "AI") nearly doubled in a year, from 8 to 15 percent. So you can expect to get a high number of applicants if you go live with a marketing job description.

As a founder, staying on top of functional trends will help you hire someone who can stay with you for the long haul, and guide you in asking the right questions and evaluating the right skills in the process.

## The rise of the generalists

One of the key findings is that demand for specialists who are great at one thing is winding down in favor of AI-powered generalists. The tasks companies used to build whole job titles around are the ones AI already handles alone or nearly alone. Email marketing tops that list. SEO, social media, copywriting, paid media, and performance analytics all need only “minimal human input” now.

![Image 1: Inc Logo](https://www.inc.com/_public/newsletters/inc_this_morning.svg)

This Morning

The daily digest for entrepreneurs and business leaders

I’ve experienced this compression in my own team. As an M-shaped C-level marketer—meaning I have deep expertise in a few areas and general knowledge of a few more—my team is about half the size it was at the start of the year, and each team member is working across more fields. The social-media marketer is now doing ad copy and brainstorming campaign ideas, while our video editor is now acting as the company’s creative strategist. I’m spending a lot more time in [AI tools](https://www.inc.com/tor-constantino/7-free-ai-tools-to-help-founders-save-time-cut-costs-and-boost-productivity/91187333 "ai tools") setting the foundation and working on training materials and mentoring the team on how to level up in areas where there’s an expressed need.

When designing a role description, think about the broader skills rather than a specific sub-discipline of marketing. For example, copywriting cuts across SEO, product descriptions, email marketing, ad copy, social-media captions and scripts, etc. So finding a really strong copywriter and pairing them with a really strong M-shaped strategist who’s worked across some of the aforementioned disciplines will be a strong team because you have both a strategist and a practitioner who can work together and rely on each other’s expertise to check each other’s work.

## Test candidates on a real AI workflow, not a checklist

A lot of my coaching and fractional CMO founder clients have run into trouble with their marketing hires because they just ask “How comfortable are you with AI tools?” and trust the candidate’s answers. The delta between someone who knows how to write a basic, mediocre prompt and someone who actually understands how to get the most out of generative and agentic AI tools is Grand Canyon-sized now.

Title: How to measure the true value of creators and review content

URL Source: https://searchengineland.com/value-creators-review-content-485028

Published Time: 2026-08-21T13:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Review content creators — including YouTubers, websites, and social media personalities — can add significant value, even if some long-term effects become parasitic.

By **parasitic**, I mean something specific: over time, a review publisher may continue earning commissions from customers who already knew about the brand, were researching it, or were otherwise already in its sales funnel. In those cases, the review may still build trust and help close the sale, but it no longer primarily serves as a means of customer acquisition.

This is where proper measurement and coordination across marketing teams become essential.

Review creators work with:

*   Affiliate marketing
*   PR
*   AEO/GEO
*   SEO (I separate this from AEO and GEO now, as the skills and techniques are similar but different enough for their own channels)
*   Brand
*   Social media marketers
*   Influencer managers

In many companies, these teams aren’t talking to each other.

The PR team pays a media fee and sends the product. The affiliate manager then adds the creator to the affiliate program, allowing them to earn commissions on top of the media fee they’ve already received.

Next, the AEO/GEO team sees the publisher being cited or sourced and decides to pursue more coverage. Then the social media team notices the creator’s growing momentum and begins collaborating with them and amplifying their content.

The problem is that the company may have created much of that momentum itself.

A publisher can still provide real value. But when teams operate independently, a company can end up paying multiple times for the same relationship, then mistake the resulting visibility for organic third-party validation.

That’s why incrementality matters.

An affiliate platform can tell you a publisher participated in a transaction. It can’t necessarily tell you whether that publisher caused the transaction or whether the customer would have purchased anyway.

Before addressing incrementality, though, many teams also need a stronger understanding of the FTC’s rules and guidance on reviews, endorsements, and disclosing material connections, including sponsorships, affiliate relationships, pay-to-post arrangements, free products, and other forms of compensation.

Before working with creators, familiarize yourself with the [FTC’s Endorsement Guides FAQ](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking), the [FTC’s Endorsement Guides](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/07/26/2023-14795/guides-concerning-the-use-of-endorsements-and-testimonials-in-advertising), and the FTC’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule. Then consult a licensed attorney about the best practices for your company.

This applies whether you’re working with Reddit users, TikTok creators, YouTubers, bloggers, media companies, or other reviewers.

The value of review content depends on your team’s goals. Below are some of its primary use cases, along with the benefits, drawbacks, and attribution considerations to help you incorporate review content into your company’s strategy.

*   Combating negative PR and misinformation
*   Driving initial sales while creating potential long-term margin leakage
*   Building trust through credible third-party validation
*   Strengthening AEO/GEO signals and increasing visibility
*   Shaping how people understand your brand
*   Increasing conversion rates on your website and in advertising

## Combating negative PR and misinformation

One benefit of investing in review content—through affiliate, brand, PR, or influencer partnerships—is creating accurate, up-to-date third-party content that can compete with negative, outdated, or misleading information about your brand in search results and AI-assisted discovery tools like ChatGPT and Claude.

Many review creators require the freedom to share both the positives and the negatives. Brands can still ask creators to cover factual talking points, product features, compatibility, or specific testing scenarios, as long as creators remain free to share their honest experiences and conclusions.

Examples include:

*   Correcting myths and inaccurate claims
*   Explaining compatibility
*   Demonstrating new features, services, or use cases
*   Addressing false claims by showing what the product or service actually does

*   **Tip:** If you want a new review to compete with older or negative content, promote it. Amplify it through advertising, feature or embed it on your website when appropriate, and support it with SEO and AEO/GEO efforts.

Paid promotion alone won’t cause a review to rank in Google or become an AI citation. The goal is to make genuinely useful content easier to discover and give it more opportunities to earn visibility.

You can measure the impact through higher conversion rates, customer reviews that mention specific use cases (such as “it works for XYZ”), and fewer live chat or customer support questions about particular features, compatibility, or intended uses.

## Initial sales increases with potential future margin losses

When a review first goes live, it reaches the creator’s subscribers and regular audience. If it generates comments, shares, likes, or other engagement, it may continue gaining visibility and introducing new customers through search, YouTube recommendations, social platforms, and other discovery channels.

Over time, though, the economics can change.

If the review is viewed primarily by people already searching for your brand, comparing products they already know, or otherwise showing purchase intent, affiliate commissions may increasingly represent margin leakage rather than customer acquisition.

For example, if a review appears in Google, an AI-generated answer, YouTube, or another discovery platform and includes an affiliate link, you may end up paying commissions on customers who were already in your sales funnel.

That doesn’t make the review worthless.

It may still build trust, answer objections, demonstrate the product, and increase the likelihood of conversion. But that’s different from acquiring a customer who had never heard of your brand.

That’s why attribution alone isn’t enough.

A publisher generating $100,000 in attributed affiliate revenue doesn’t necessarily mean your company would lose $100,000 in sales if that publisher disappeared.

Instead, ask questions like:

*   Was the customer new to the brand?
*   Had they already visited your website?
*   Had they searched for your brand before finding the review?
*   Were they already an email subscriber or existing customer?
*   Was the review the first meaningful touchpoint or one of the last before conversion?
*   Would they have purchased without the affiliate review?

If customer reviews or non-affiliate creators appear for the same searches and provide the same confidence, you may retain more margin because you aren’t paying a recurring commission every time someone converts.

This is what I mean when I say review content can become parasitic from an attribution perspective.

Instead of relying exclusively on affiliate reviews, you can also work with creators on flat-fee arrangements and encourage authentic customer reviews, where you aren’t paying a commission every time the content is viewed, clicked, and leads to a sale.

That doesn’t mean affiliate reviews are a bad investment. It means they should be evaluated based on incremental value, not just the revenue attributed to them by an affiliate platform.

## Trust from a credible third party

Whether it’s a media brand or a microinfluencer, seeing a product or service demonstrated through images and video can add credibility.

The person can watch as the product arrives or a service provider begins, see the full process of it being used or the work being done, and visualize the end result as the reviewer shows the completed solution.

If it worked for the reviewer, the potential customer can better understand whether it might work for them too.

This is where a lot of the value comes from.

A thoughtful review provides third-party evidence that your products or services can work in a real-world use case and can help a potential customer understand why your business might be a solution for their needs.

The credibility of the reviewer matters here.

A media company or influencer is not automatically trustworthy simply because they have an audience. Their value comes from things like actual testing, expertise, transparency, honest opinions, clear disclosures, a relevant audience, and a history of producing useful information.

## AEO/GEO signals for increased exposure

While I don’t expect today’s tactics to work forever, I’m currently seeing niche creators and influential websites appear to influence AI-generated answers and recommendations.

When affiliate sites, media companies, YouTube creators, and social media influencers publish reviews and listicles, I’ve observed some of the brands we track appearing more often across AI-assisted search and answer engines.

That’s an observation and correlation—not proof that paying for the coverage caused the increase.

One possible explanation is retrieval.

Many AI search and answer systems retrieve current information from the web when responding to users. As a result, third-party reviews, comparisons, videos, and articles can become source material when these systems evaluate which products fit a particular use case.

That doesn’t mean this happens in every industry or on every platform.

But when legitimate third-party publishers accurately discuss your product’s features, benefits, compatibility, and use cases, they create more content connecting your brand with those concepts.

I’ve also seen other marketers report similar observations.

As AI systems improve at distinguishing independent editorial coverage from paid or commercially influenced content, the value of paid reviews may change. For now, though, third-party coverage appears to provide benefits in at least some of the markets we track.

One especially interesting example is what Time has reportedly done with content served to AI crawlers.

Reporting in 2026 found that Time served machine-oriented versions of some pages to AI crawlers, including sponsored content that wasn’t necessarily presented the same way to human visitors.

That’s different from saying the content becomes training data.

Training, retrieval, grounding, and citations are separate concepts.

A crawler accessing content doesn’t prove that the information changes an AI model’s underlying training or that it will appear in an AI-generated answer. But it does raise an interesting question about marketing and disclosure.

Consider a hypothetical example.

A media company is paid to review a product or include it in an affiliate listicle. It then makes a machine-targeted version of that content available to an AI retrieval system.

Later, the AI system retrieves that information when recommending products to a consumer.

If the original source was commercially influenced but the consumer has no way of knowing that, what disclosure obligations should eventually apply?

I’m not suggesting current FTC guidance requires AI assistants to disclose commercially influenced retrieved content in that scenario. It doesn’t establish a general requirement like that today.

But it’s a question I expect regulators, platforms, publishers, and advertisers will eventually have to address as AI systems play a larger role in purchase decisions.

For marketers, the key is not to confuse these mechanisms.

Getting mentioned online may increase the information available to AI retrieval systems. That doesn’t mean you’ve “trained the LLM,” and it doesn’t guarantee the system will retrieve, cite, or recommend your brand.

## Shaping how people understand your brand

One of the most valuable aspects of reviews isn’t just countering negative public opinion. It’s ensuring the right use cases and benefits are represented when people research your brand.

If you sell an undershirt, different audiences may value it for different reasons. You can influence how it’s presented so reviews resonate with the customers who care most about specific benefits.

An undershirt is just a piece of clothing, but parents may want to know whether it’s tagless so it won’t itch or scratch their children’s skin. A budget-conscious customer may care more about durability than style, while a fashion-focused customer may value how well it blends with or complements signature pieces.

It’s the same product, but each creator and audience may see its value differently.

As AI-powered and traditional search systems deliver more personalized and specific answers, these niche reviews become more valuable because they create explicit third-party connections between a product and particular audiences, needs, attributes, and use cases.

More importantly, they help consumers determine whether your brand solves their specific problem.

*   **Tip:**Encourage review partners to create honest comparison content that explains your brand’s strengths and tradeoffs. This can help consumers searching for queries like “which is better” or “which should I use.”

The key is honesty. Asking a creator to cover specific factual features is very different from asking them to reach a predetermined conclusion.

## Increasing conversions on your website and in ads

One thing we do with clients is embed reviews on product, category, and landing pages. With permission, we also use them in advertising.

We’ve consistently seen product demonstrations from real people and media companies increase conversions because potential customers can see a product or service in use rather than relying solely on the company’s claims.

Any company can claim it has a solution. Review partners can provide third-party evidence that the solution worked in a real-world use case.

This is one of the biggest sources of value, even when some affiliate sales come from customers who were already in the funnel.

You may also reduce production costs by repurposing creator videos in paid social campaigns when your agreement includes the necessary paid media usage rights.

The creator can continue growing their audience and earning affiliate commissions, while your company uses that content to convert the portion of your audience that still needs additional proof before buying.

Review content becomes parasitic when its ongoing affiliate commissions come primarily from customers who were already going to buy. That doesn’t mean the content has stopped creating value.

With our clients, we identify which creators and media companies are working with each team, then build a measurement framework that tracks those relationships across channels and gives the company a more complete view of their impact.

That allows us to ensure important product use cases are represented, encourage creators to remain honest in their reviews, expand awareness by amplifying valuable content with paid media, and increase conversions by giving potential customers credible third-party evidence that the brand may solve their problem.

The mistake is treating all attributed affiliate revenue as customer acquisition.

Review content serves different purposes over its lifecycle. Early on, it may introduce a brand to a creator’s audience and generate incremental customers. Later, the same review may function primarily as comparison content, social proof, objection handling, reputation support, or a final trust-building touchpoint before conversion.

Those roles still create value. They just shouldn’t all be measured the same way.
